content.text: When a prompt says "cite your sources", the citations Claude writes are generated text like the rest of the answer: nothing checks that the section exists or that the quote is in your document. The Citations feature is different: you send documents with
enabled, and the API returns each cited passage as structured data with a valid pointer into your documents. It still can't promise the passage proves the claim, so your code checks that part.

Your HR assistant answers employee questions from the handbook, and its system prompt says "Cite every claim as [Handbook §x.y]". A contractor asks about the annual bonus and gets: "Contractors with 12 months of service are eligible [Handbook §4.2]." HR opens §4.2 and finds the parental leave policy. The handbook says bonuses are for employees only. The answer looked exactly like the hundreds of correct ones, with the same confident bracket at the end, and nothing in the pipeline could tell them apart.
"Asking Claude in the prompt to cite sources yields citations that reliably point to real passages in your documents." There are good reasons to believe it:

items.text: Claude follows formatting instructions well, so every answer comes back with neat, consistent references.
Spot checks pass: most prompted citations are right, which makes the wrong ones rare and easy to miss.
recommends asking Claude to quote and cite.
A reference with a section number and quote marks looks like something a system verified.

content.text: The half-truth: asking for quotes is a real

technique. The same guide says these techniques "significantly reduce hallucinations", and adds that "they don't eliminate them entirely". A prompted citation makes an answer easier to audit by hand. It doesn't give your code anything it can trust.
A prompted citation is just more output

When you ask for "[Handbook §4.2]", Claude writes those characters the way it writes every other word. Nothing in the API compares them with your document. A section number can be wrong, a "quote" can be a paraphrase, and the format can drift. To use them in a product, you'd parse references out of prose with a regular expression and search the source for each quote yourself, and you'd still have no answer when the quote doesn't match exactly.
The Citations feature returns pointers, not prose
With the Citations feature, the sources go in as
, and the API does the bookkeeping:
Plain text and PDFs are split into sentences; custom content documents keep the blocks you provide, with no further chunking. A chunk is the smallest thing Claude can cite.
blocks. A block that makes a claim from your documents carries a
and a location: character range for plain text, page range for PDFs, block range for custom content.
Here is one cited block, as the docs show it:
Because the API parses the citations and extracts
itself, the docs state that they "are guaranteed to contain valid pointers to the provided documents".
also doesn't count toward output tokens, so if you used to ask Claude to copy quotes out, you might pay less.

A valid pointer means the passage exists, at that location, in that document. It doesn't mean the passage supports the sentence it's attached to; that's still Claude's judgment. Anthropic reports that in its evaluations the feature is "significantly more likely to cite the most relevant quotes" than prompting, which is better, not perfect. And not every block gets a citation. Joining text has none, and neither does a claim Claude didn't draw from your documents. In the docs' own words about extracted fields, "The API doesn't guarantee either", meaning a value and a citation for each one.
The first version asks for citations in the prompt. The second sends the handbook as a document and reads the citations the API returns:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
reply = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=2048,
    system="Answer from the handbook. Cite every claim as [Handbook §x.y].",
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": f"<handbook>{HANDBOOK}</handbook>\n{QUESTION}"}],
)
answer = next(b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text")
print(answer)  # "[Handbook §4.2]" is text Claude wrote; nothing checked it

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
reply = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=2048,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "document", "title": "Employee Handbook 2026",
         "source": {"type": "text", "media_type": "text/plain",
                    "data": HANDBOOK},
         "citations": {"enabled": True}},
        {"type": "text", "text": QUESTION},
    ]}],
)
for block in reply.content:
    if block.type == "text":
        quotes = [c.cited_text for c in block.citations or []]
        print(repr(block.text), "<-", quotes or "no citation")

content.text: The second version prints each piece of the answer next to the exact handbook sentences behind it, and the pieces with no citation are easy to spot, flag or hide.

content.text: Citations can't be combined with structured outputs: a request that enables citations and sets

returns a 400. A prompt that asks for only JSON still succeeds, but the docs warn the response "might contain few or no citations". For structured data, ask for one line per field, cite each line, and parse the lines yourself.
reaches Claude but is never cited, so
is a good place for metadata. Sentence chunks don't suit bullet lists or transcripts; a custom content document lets you decide what one citable unit is. In a RAG pipeline,
blocks give the same citations with your own source and title.
How to apply it in your project
Search your prompts for "cite", "source" and "quote", and your code for regexes that parse references out of answers.

A factual sentence without a citation is a signal: flag it, hide it, or send it for review.
On a sample of answers, check that each
actually supports its sentence. A valid pointer can still point at the wrong passage.

The Citations feature returns structured locations whose pointers are guaranteed valid, plus
that doesn't count toward output tokens.
A valid pointer isn't proof: whether the passage supports the claim is still Claude's judgment.
Uncited text blocks exist, so decide in code what to do with claims that have no citation.
Citations and structured outputs don't mix; use one line per field when you need both.
